diagnosis:
The calibrated model reaches a daily NSE of 0.76 over 1971–1997 (KGE 0.86, PBIAS −1%, r 0.88). This is a fit to the calibration period only. I did not run a split-sample validation.

The Ver is a chalk catchment fed by groundwater. Observed runoff is about 0.22 mm/day, only about 12% of rainfall, and the observed flow is very smooth (maximum 1.06 mm/day). Even if evaporation ran at the full potential rate, standard HBV would leave too much water, so it cannot close this water balance. The first plain calibration had a bias of +58% and an NSE of −0.4.

To fix this, I used the lower groundwater store as a sink. I set its outflow rate K2 to about 2e-6, so it barely drains. The percolation rate (PERC ≈ 0.39 mm/day) then acts as a loss to deep or outside-catchment groundwater. In the final 1400-run search, K2, PERC and the soil parameters (BETA, FC, LP) moved little. The upper store plays the chalk aquifer: it drains very slowly (K1 ≈ 0.0032, a timescale of about 300 days) and only gives quick flow when it holds more than about 72 mm.

The soil store is large (FC ≈ 1080 mm) with a low LP (0.23), so evaporation stays close to potential. Snow parameters are poorly constrained but hardly matter.

Weaknesses: storm peaks from urban runoff (20% of the area) are poorly captured. Low flows during droughts, such as 1976 and 1990–92, depend on the constant loss term. The start-of-run stores are set to the model's end-1997 state (low after the 1996–97 drought). I'm moderately confident in the parameters, because the sink structure is a workaround rather than a physical process.
